action_summary: A sentence that names a DEFINITION to move was answered by a FILE command. Measured on main e304434033 with big.py holding a, b and c: "Move b from <b>/big.py into <b>/out.py." bound shell.command.run argv ['mv', big.py, out.py] -- overwriting out.py with the source's bytes and DELETING big.py -- and reported PASS__RAW_GOAL_EXECUTED_AND_EXACT_SEMANTIC_ACCEPTANCE_VERIFIED. The rule that refuses a file command for a named definition only fired when the sentence used the word 'function'; without it, nothing matched and the file died for a request about one function in it. "Copy b from A into B" was the same mistake without the deletion: the whole file was copied and certified. The row that answers the move existed all along -- python.refactor.move_symbol.v1 -- and now receives it: b leaves big.py, a and c stay, and the door reports the row it used. The discriminator is the sentence's grammar, not another noun list: in 'move|copy <OBJECT> from <SOURCE> ... <DESTINATION>' the OBJECT is what moves, and a file command can only be the answer when that object is a file. Copying a definition has no row and now refuses instead of copying the file; a real file move ('Move <path> to <path>') is unchanged. Measured after: the same sentence PASSes through move_symbol, and the ordinary-sentence SWE matrix is 6/6 with its module-split row down from 3.9 s to 336 ms.
